extracted.intended_audience: writers (fiction, nonfiction, essayists) and aspiring comedians
extracted.subtask_description: A short prescriptive piece extracting seven practical rules from Jerry Seinfeld and Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee about developing material, sustaining practice, and improving craft for writers and comedy writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always Be Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians are always writing; keep ideas in perpetual progress and capture thoughts as they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry a notebook or phone app to jot ideas; write while waiting (in lines, haircuts, before movies), dictate into your phone at a red light. Maintain multiple drafts in progress so ideas can marinate while you develop others. Example: Seinfeld worked on a single joke for two years while also creating and editing many other jokes. Anti-patterns: waiting for inspiration before writing; spending very long periods on a single piece without working on anything else. Quote: “Comedy writing is something you don’t see people doing. It’s a secretive thing.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep Your Eyes Open
rubrics_metrics.description: Train yourself to notice the details of life and convert observations into material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be receptive to small moments: overheard conversations can become lines of dialogue, mannerisms can inform characters, everyday oddities can spark ideas. Practice active observation like a 'well-trained spy'—listen to waitstaff comments, notice where a check is set, overhear table conversations. Quote: “Funny is the world I live in. You’re funny, I’m interested. You’re not funny, I’m interested.” Anti-pattern: not paying attention to surroundings or dismissing small details as unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy the Little Things
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with present moments and personal experience rather than observing life only from a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value experiences themselves (time with friends, small routines) as fuel for writing; living full lives supplies richer material than detached note-taking alone. Example: the author finding diners and morning gatherings to be 'treasure troves' of inspiration but valuing the hour with friends even more. Anti-pattern: treating observation as purely data collection without participating in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t Be Afraid to Get Real
rubrics_metrics.description: Inject authenticity and personal experience into your writing—even uncomfortable or self-deprecating material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal hardships, relationships, and real emotions to add depth and capture readers' attention. Writers can pursue outcomes beyond laughter—knowledge, insight, emotion—by pouring themselves into work. Examples: Sarah Silverman turning cancer into a special; Chris Rock using his ended marriage as material. Anti-pattern: keeping every piece emotionally distant or purely detached from the author's lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get Angry
rubrics_metrics.description: Harness anger and annoyance as a powerful source of material and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what annoys or enrages you and 'run with it'—write rants, satire, or create characters who embody the irritating trait to provoke reader reaction. Quote: “All good comedy comes from a place of anger. Figure out what’s making you angry and work on it from there.” Anti-pattern: avoiding strong emotion entirely or sanitizing work to the point of blandness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Your Friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop material with a trusted, critical circle rather than only seeking affirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share drafts with friends who will both support and critically evaluate your work; polish material with that group before wider exposure. Beware of only-affirmation friends—seek honest, relevant feedback. The path includes grinding (performing for free, iterating) before earning pay. Quote: The Four Levels of Comedy: 'Make your friends laugh, Make strangers laugh, Get paid to make strangers laugh, Make people talk like you because it’s so fun.' Anti-pattern: skipping iterative feedback or relying solely on praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never Settle
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously seek new challenges and diversify your craft rather than recycling the same work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue new genres, formats, and subjects to promote growth—try nonfiction if you write fiction, attempt poetry, or create characters far from your comfort zone. Avoid doing only what you've already proven you can do; stagnation is likened to 'the road to death.' Anti-pattern: remaining in a comfort zone and repeatedly producing the same type of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Confident About Grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and correct grammar in all written communications before sending or publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread every email, essay, or story for grammar mistakes and fix them prior to sending/publishing. This is a practical finishing standard to maintain professionalism; no extended examples provided.
